We formulate symmetry defects dressed by topological quantum field theories for flavor symmetries including finite non-Abelian flavor transformations with rational anomaly characters and modular flavor symmetries with the rational part of modular anomaly cocycles, for gauge sectors with the required exact higher-form symmetry. As a concrete example, we construct a Froggatt-Nielsen (FN) model in which an order-four subgroup $\mathbb Z_4^{\rm FN}\subset U(1)_{\rm FN}$ is completed into a non-invertible defect through its mixed anomaly with an intermediate hidden $U(1)_H$ gauge sector in the infrared monopole-decoupling limit. The non-invertible FN symmetry can be explicitly broken at the energy scale where monopoles become dynamical. This breaking from the infrared viewpoint can be realized in an ultraviolet hidden $SU(2)_H$ theory as instanton effects, where a constrained instanton with topological charge one generates a fermion mixing term that violates FN charge by one unit. Its coefficient contains the nonperturbative factor $ζ_H\sim\exp[-8π^2/g_H^2(v_H)]$. When independent FN-breaking terms are subleading, integrating out the heavy fermions gives $(Y_ν)_{ij}\proptoζ_Hε^{\ell_i+n_j}$ in a rotated basis for the right-handed neutrinos, to leading order in the instanton-induced fermion mixing. The nonperturbative factor provides the exponential suppression of the neutrino Yukawa couplings, while the FN charges determine the powers of $ε$. For the chosen FN charges and generic order-one coefficients, $m_2/m_3\simε$, favoring normal ordering. An independent $\mathbb Z_8^D$ gauge symmetry forbids Majorana masses. The same FN charge assignment reproduces the leading quark and charged-lepton Yukawa hierarchies.

title: Novel high-pressure silicon allotrope with quartz topology from first principles
authors: Samir F. Matar, Vladimir L. Solozhenko
abstract: A novel silicon allotrope, qtz Si, with quartz topology is proposed and investigated alongside four known allotropes (dia Si-I, lon Si-IV, bsn Si-II, and gsi Si-III) using first-principles density functional theory. qtz Si is found to exhibit the smallest atom-averaged volume (18.06 A3), highest density (2.582 g/cm3), highest bulk modulus (98 GPa), and highest maximum phonon frequency (16 THz) among the five, while showing the lowest shear modulus (37 GPa). All five allotropes are confirmed to satisfy the Born stability criteria and to display positive phonon frequencies throughout the Brillouin zone, i.e., they are mechanically and dynamically stable. Electronic structure calculations show that qtz Si is a semimetal with a vanishing gap, whereas dia Si and lon Si are semiconductors, and bsn and gsi allotropes are weakly metallic. Energy-volume equations of state place gsi and qtz 0.11-0.15 eV/atom above dia, bsn, and lon, consistent with their identification as high-pressure or metastable phases.

title: ConStore: Search-Overlapped Prefetch and Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Storage for Disk-Based ANNS
authors: Zhutao Zhuang, Nong Xiao, Zhiguang Chen, Yue Yu
abstract: Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search, recommendation, and advertising over corpora that exceed memory capacity. Existing ANNS research often focuses on vector search at small top-K, whereas industrial-scale applications require larger retrieval sets. Fetching the corresponding content from storage remains comparatively underexplored. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector corpora shows that, at large K, content fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency and cannot be ignored in end-to-end retrieval. We present ConStore, a content storage engine combining two complementary techniques to reduce end-to-end retrieval latency. Speculative Inline Content Prefetch (SICP) commonly abstracts graph-based and cluster-based ANNS as progressive SSD I/O that refines an in-flight candidate queue. It prefetches content for stable leading candidates under a bounded I/O budget, overlapping content reads with search without changing the final top-K results. Co-Retrieval-Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG) uses query logs to place frequently co-retrieved documents in contiguous segments. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) adapts this layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget. Group Content Fetch (GCF) exploits this layout to coalesce per-document random reads into batched, page-aware I/O requests. SICP works independently of the content layout, while RPAG and GCF reduce fetch cost even without prefetching. Across three multi-hop QA workloads with K from 10 to 1600, ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency over the best per-document-read baseline by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN. Separate experiments on 100M- and billion-vector indexes demonstrate SICP's applicability at larger scales.

title: Defect Candidates for Single-Photon Emission in Monolayer GaS and GaSe
authors: Michael Lorke
abstract: We investigate the spin-resolved electronic structure of native vacancies and substitutional defects in monolayer GaS and GaSe using an anisotropic screened-exchange functional developed for two-dimensional material systems. By combining an energy-based classification of defect-associated states with spatially resolved projections and partial charge densities, we examine how these defects modify the in-gap electronic structure and assess their relevance for defect-based single-photon emission. The results identify gallium vacancies, particularly in GaS, as candidates single-photon emitters.

title: Effect of deuteration on methane cluster stability
authors: Ake Andersson, Klavs Hansen, Siegfried Kollotzek, Johannes Reichegger, Paul Scheier
abstract: The evaporation from clusters of mixed deuterated and protonated methane molecules has been studied experimentally and theoretically. Only loss of the two components CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ is observed, showing the absence of hydrogen scrambling. The branching ratio of the two channels scales with the mole fractions of the isotopologues, corresponding to a fixed ratio of 1.5 for the CH$_4$ and CD$_4$ rates. The number is explained by the combined effect of the zero-point energies found in quantum chemical calculations and the use of detailed balance to describe the evaporation process, the latter by incorporating the moment of inertia of the two isotopologue molecules and their rotational degrees of freedom. The difference in evaporative activation energies is determined to be 6.1~\% and 6.8~\% from two experimental determinations and 8.7~\% theoretically with B3LYP+GD3BJ, corresponding to 5--7~meV. The same theory finds the CH$_4$ activation energy to be 83.8 meV, close to the experimental bulk value of 84.7 meV. Differences in Helmholtz free energies of decay products are extracted from the experimental data, yielding the molecular mixing as the only contribution to the entropy term.

title: Distribution Functions and Moments of Harmonically Trapped Inertial Run-and-Tumble Particles in a Shear-Thickening Medium
authors: Subhanker Howlader, Prasenjit Das
abstract: We study the dynamics of an athermal inertial active particle confined in a harmonic potential and moving through shear-thickening media in one dimension. The activity is modeled using a symmetric dichotomous noise of strength $Σ$ and flipping rate $λ$, which mimics a run-and-tumble particle. The shear-thickening response of the medium is incorporated through a velocity-dependent viscous force of the form $g(v) \sim \tan(v)$. Starting from the Fokker-Planck equations corresponding to the particle's dynamics, we numerically compute the time-dependent joint probability density function $f(x,v,t)$ using a finite-volume upwind scheme. Next, we numerically solve the particle's equations of motion to obtain the steady-state position $P_s(x)$ and velocity $W_s(v)$ distributions and compare them with the marginal distributions obtained from $f(x,v,t)$ at sufficiently large $t$. The two approaches show excellent agreement. Both $P_s(x)$ and $W_s(v)$ exhibit several intriguing transitions as $λ$ is varied, and they eventually approach Gaussian-like profiles at sufficiently large $λ$. Our study of the time-dependent position-velocity correlation, $\langle xv \rangle(t)$, shows that larger values of $λ$ lead to faster relaxation to the steady state when all other parameters are held constant.

title: A simple classification of the special matchings in the symmetric group
authors: Fabrizio Caselli, Mario Marietti
abstract: We establish a simple characterization of special matchings of all Bruhat intervals in the symmetric group, yielding an explicit classification that depends only on the one-line notations of the endpoints. We also study extensions of graded posets by partial special matchings, proving the existence and uniqueness of such extensions and providing an explicit construction. Combining these results, we obtain a combinatorial algorithm for computing Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials for an isomorphism-closed family of Bruhat intervals that includes all intervals whose bottom element has length at most one.

title: Spurious Attention Heads in Vision Transformers: Mechanistic Identification of Annotation-Driven Bias in Medical Chest X-Ray Analysis
authors: Joshua Muhumuza, Cornelius Kalenzi
abstract: Vision Transformers deployed in medical imaging exploit spurious correlations, yet the internal mechanisms remain unidentified and impossible to fix. We apply mechanistic interpretability to locate one such mechanism in ViT-Base 16: a single attention head (L8H10) that functions as a dedicated annotation-reader on chest X-rays, attending to corner text rather than lung pathology in 62% of 200 COVID-19 images. Causal validation via inpainting confirms annotation content rather than luminance or edge density drives the behaviour, increasing lung attention 1.52 times upon removal in affected images ($p{<}0.0001$). The finding replicates across NIH ChestX-ray14 (79%), DeiT-Base (88%), and ViT-Large 16 (80%), establishing spurious annotation-attending heads as a consistent property of ViT-family architectures across two datasets and three architectures. Full fine-tuning does not suppress the behaviour and may entrench it: 98.4% of spurious images remain spurious and the spurious rate rises marginally, as the shortcut is reinforced rather than removed. Critically, single-head ablation produces $p{=}0.340$ and multi-head ablation of all three identified carriers produces $p{=}0.532$, meaning a causally verified annotation-reading circuit is completely invisible to output-level evaluation. Mechanistic auditing finds what behavioural testing cannot.

title: Characterisations for coarse embeddability via quasi-locality and Schur multipliers
authors: Kang Li, Jiawen Zhang, Jingming Zhu
abstract: We establish three new characterisations of coarse embeddability into Hilbert space for discrete metric spaces of bounded geometry, in terms of escaping quasi-local couplings, Schur multipliers, and operator norm state localisation. As applications, we prove that if a sparse metric space of bounded geometry is coarsely embeddable into Hilbert space, then every ghost projection in the quasi-local algebra is compact, while we also provide a counterexample to the converse implication. Finally, we characterise coarse embeddability into Hilbert space via the relative Haagerup property for the quasi-local algebra, and investigate its relation to coarse embeddability into $\ell^p$ for $p>2$.

title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhixu Li, Keqian Tang, Litian Gong, Jingyu Yao, Wenqian Zhang, Tianze Xu, Zehao Wang, Yuping Wang, Junge Zhang, Jiachen Li
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
authors: Wenye Yu, Yijin Chen, Kaiyi Xiong, Wenbo Han, Wendi Chen, Yang Jin, Han Xue, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Chuan Wen
abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.

title: Uniform estimates for elliptic systems with critical Sobolev coefficients
authors: Tian Lan
abstract: The $W^{1,p}$ estimate for uniformly elliptic operators of divergence form with VMO coefficients is classical. In particular, this provides $W^{1,p}$ estimates for elliptic operators with coefficients in $W^{1,n}$. However, this theory does not yield constants in the estimates controlled by the $W^{1,n}$ norm of the coefficients, since the total $W^{1,n}$ norm does not control the rate of decay for the mean oscillation. In this work, we establish uniform estimates for divergence-form elliptic systems whose coefficients lie in the critical Sobolev--Lorentz spaces $W^{1,(n,s)}$ with $1\le s<\infty$, have an $L^\infty$-bounded spatially symmetric part, and satisfy an integral ellipticity condition. The constant in the estimate is controlled by the corresponding norms of coefficients and the ellipticity constant.

title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
authors: Tianjiao Yu, Zhilin Ou, Yifan Shen, Xinzhuo Li, Yuanzhe Liu, Onkar Kishor Susladkar, Fan Wang, Ismini Lourentzou
abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
authors: Han Su, Meng Tian, Tianyu Huang, Mingyu Gao, Lennox Wei, Dongxu Li, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaohe Wu, Wangmeng Zuo
abstract: Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial supervision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token's input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model's native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28). RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, while the full model preserves general video understanding. Project page: https://sumuru789.github.io/DK-VLM-website/.

title: On exponential sums with multiplicative coefficients
authors: Haozhe Gou
abstract: Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\leq1}$ be multiplicative, and suppose that $α$ has a rational approximation $a/q$ with $|α-a/q|\leq 1/(qx)$ and $q\leq x/((\log x)^2(\log\log x)^3)$. We prove that $\left|\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)e(nα)\right|\leq \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q} +O\left(\frac{x}{\log x}\right)$, whereas complete multiplicativity improves $4/\sqrt6$ to $1$. Both constants are optimal. In particular, this confirms a folklore conjecture on exponential sums with multiplicative coefficients motivated by the work of Montgomery and Vaughan (1977). We also obtain logarithmically weighted estimates and give counterexamples to related conjectures.

title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
authors: Shangheng Du, Jinxin Shi, Shuaiyu Zhang, Yiming Wu, Junpeng Zhao, Shiyang Feng, Xin Li, Liang He, Xiangchao Yan, Bo Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

title: Stratification of opers with apparent singularities and isomonodromic bubbling
authors: Duong Dinh, Troy Figiel, Joerg Teschner
abstract: On a compact Riemann surface of genus $g \geq 2$, we study Simpson's stratification of the de Rham moduli space of rank-2 flat connections. Upon representing flat $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$-connections by branched projective structures, or equivalently by opers with apparent singularities, the stratum containing a flat connection is determined by the minimal number of apparent singularities needed to represent it. We construct explicit holomorphic families in which two simple apparent singularities collide and disappear, so that the family crosses into a smaller stratum; this realizes Simpson's closure relation between strata near generic points. The analogous families of Higgs bundles are described by Baker--Akhiezer divisors on the spectral curve in which two points converge to a pair of points exchanged by the spectral involution. We show that, before the collision, the two apparent singularities are joined by twin paths bounding a bubble, so that these families arise from the isomonodromic bubbling surgery discussed by Calsamiglia, Deroin and Francaviglia.

title: Dense4D: Pixel-Level 4D Human Correspondence
authors: Rıza Alp Güler
abstract: Reconstructing human motion in 4D requires identifying the same surface points through articulation, deformation and changes in visibility. We introduce Dense4D, to our knowledge the first feed-forward model dedicated to dense 4D correspondence across the body, clothing and hair from a set of monocular RGB images, without a body template. Trained specifically for human geometry, Dense4D jointly processes person-centred crops with known image-to-crop transforms to predict Human Point Maps (HPMs) and depth for each image. An HPM assigns each person pixel the 3D position of its observed surface point at a common reference time. These maps support amodal correspondence: points hidden in the reference image can be localised from observations in other frames. Matching HPM coordinates across crops establishes correspondence without predicting camera poses or large scene displacements; per-image depth then lifts the matches into 3D tracks. Experiments on real people demonstrate substantially higher tracking accuracy and closer agreement with scanned surfaces than the evaluated baselines. Points from different frames assemble into coherent human geometry in the reference pose, providing visible evidence of consistent dense correspondence through articulation and clothing deformation. Additional qualitative results, videos, and an interactive viewer are available at https://alpguler.com/dense4d.

title: An Optimal Gap-Majority Lemma for Bounded Rounds Communication
authors: Pachara Sawettamalya
abstract: Recent work of Sawettamalya and Yu (FOCS 2026) initiated the study of \emph{gap-majority} composition in randomized communication. They showed that if computing a $\{\pm 1\}$-valued function $f$ in $r$ rounds requires $I$ bits of information, then distinguishing $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\geq 0.01\sqrt{n}$ from $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\leq -0.01\sqrt{n}$ in $r$ rounds requires $n \cdot (I-O(\log n))$ bits of information. They also conjectured that the $O(\log n)$-additive ``loss'' can be further reduced to $O(1)$. In this note, we record that a minor adaptation to their approach combining with a finer analysis achieves the conjectured $O(1)$ loss, establishing a gap-majority lemma for bounded-round communication that is optimal up to constant factors.

title: Extended strange metal and superconductivity in partially filled moiré Hubbard bands
authors: Yiyu Xia, Yichi Zhang, Zhongdong Han, Hongyuan Li, Brandon Bauer, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Wenjin Zhao, Jie Shan, Kin Fai Mak
abstract: Moiré semiconductors provide a physical realization of the Hubbard model. Bandwidth-tuned Mott transitions and complex phase diagrams mimicking those of high-temperature superconductors have been demonstrated near a weak Mott insulating state at half-band-filling. The platform also provides an opportunity to explore the physics of a partially filled Hubbard band at doping densities far away from the Mott insulator, a regime that has remained largely unexplored. Here we report the emergence of an extended strange metal (ESM), in both doping density and twist angle, in a partially filled Hubbard band of twisted bilayer WSe2. The ESM is in the clean limit, persists down to 100mK, and spans over multiple symmetry-breaking ground states; it also appears only at small twist angles, where electronic correlations are strong. These observations distinguish the state from the reported strange metals associated with quantum criticality and favor the viewpoint that it is an intrinsic state of matter. We also report the observation of a new superconducting dome being developed from the ESM but far away from both the Mott insulating state and the van Hove singularity of the material. Our work opens the door to exploring the new regime of partially filled Hubbard bands in the clean limit.

title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking
authors: Admir Krnić, Kosta Pavlović, Petar Nedić, Željko Bolević, Slavko Kovačević, Igor Djurović
abstract: Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize. In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.

title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
authors: Arnav Chavan, Kusha Sareen, Rishabh Tiwari, Abhranil Chandra, Johan Obando-Ceron, Kurt Keutzer, Scott Niekum, Inderjit S Dhillon, Devvrit Khatri
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.

title: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents: The Role of Scaffolding
authors: Sergey Rodionov
abstract: Stronger language models may increasingly construct useful procedures for themselves, reducing the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. We investigate why this advantage persists and whether an environment-agnostic agent can be improved without environment-specific engineering. We evaluate a Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants on ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. Each variant is deployed with unchanged code, prompts, and general-purpose tools across environments, receiving environment-specific information as input. Changing only an instruction to encourage reporting difficulties and returning control for automatic continuation improves mean scores on both ARC-AGI-3 and AGI Maze, while Terminal-Bench shows small, mixed changes. Yet the general agent remains below an ARC-AGI-3-specific reference, including with GPT-5.6-sol. The reference prescribes organization and control rather than supplying new game rules or solutions. To investigate this gap, we transfer reset decisions to a scripted controller that follows a convention already given to the agent. This small change recovers part of the specialized agent's advantage. A complementary AGI Maze experiment shows that additional tutorial experience can reduce performance. Together, these findings highlight the distinction between having information and tools available and using them effectively. Supplied procedures still matter for the models tested here. The performance gains also come with higher token-based cost. The experiments do not separate better use of information and procedures from additional or differently allocated inference. We provide the EnvTraverse framework and an evaluated baseline agent for testing whether further environment-independent changes improve performance in some environments without degrading it in others.

title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
authors: Lucrezia L. Baldo, Chiara Lionello, Edward D. Donkor, Matteo Becchi, Giovanni M. Pavan
abstract: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
authors: Qingni Wang, Changdae Oh, Yuzhe Yang, Sharon Li, Jiachen Yang, Ang Li, Xin Eric Wang
abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.

title: Beyond Pairwise Repulsion: Collective Diversity via Determinant Maximization in Diffusion Sampling
authors: Kwanyoung Lee, SeungJu Cha, Yebin Ahn, Sungho Koh, Dong-Jin Kim
abstract: Strong guidance in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models concentrates sampling toward high-density modes of the conditional distribution, collapsing independently sampled noise vectors onto nearly identical visual prototypes. This limits utility for tasks that demand distributional breadth, most critically synthetic data augmentation. Diversity, however, is a collective property of the whole batch: a set can preserve every pairwise distance yet still collapse onto a low-dimensional subspace. Existing sum-of-pairwise noise-optimization and repulsion objectives respond only weakly to this higher-order failure. We propose DetNO (Determinant Noise Optimization), which formulates diverse generation as RKHS volume maximization on the initial noise, maximizing the log-determinant of an RBF Gram matrix over one-step Tweedie predictions. This set-level functional equals the squared batch volume; its repulsion is strongest when the batch is most collapsed and self-attenuates as diversity is achieved. An anchor-based fidelity term keeps the optimized noises near plausible regions, and Lagrangian relaxation gives a two-term objective with a single hyperparameter $λ$ governing the diversity-quality trade-off, without training or sampler modification. Across three backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, SD3), DetNO achieves leading intra-batch diversity in VendiScore and Mean Self-Similarity, and a downstream few-shot classification experiment confirms that broader mode coverage brings statistically significant accuracy gains for synthetic data augmentation in the low-shot regime. Fixing the pipeline and varying only the batch objective, both RBF-based aggregators outperform InfoNCE, and the log-determinant attains the best downstream accuracy on both benchmarks. Its diversity advantage over InfoNCE widens as the batch grows. Code is available at https://github.com/mobled37/DetNO.

title: Millimetre/Sub-Millimetre SETI: Expanding the Radio Technosignature Parameter Space with ALMA2040
authors: Louisa A. Mason, Michael A. Garrett, Sofia Z. Sheikh, Kelvin Wandia, Anita M. S. Richards, Vishal Gajjar, Chenoa D. Tremblay, Andrew P. V. Siemion
abstract: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) has been largely concentrated at centimetre wavelengths, and in particular in the 'water hole' (1.42-1.66 GHz) range. The millimetre and sub-millimetre sky is, by contrast, almost entirely unsearched. It also offers some natural advantages: above 35 GHz, the interstellar and interplanetary media are effectively transparent and non-dispersive, terrestrial interference is sparse, and interferometry suppresses what interference remains. Both antenna gain and usable fractional bandwidth increase with frequency, so a civilisation optimising directed, high-data-rate links has advantageous reasons to operate in this regime, as illustrated by the ongoing migration of our own telecommunications systems to much higher frequencies. Building on the first ALMA technosignature survey (Mason et al. 2025), we identify four searches ALMA2040 is uniquely placed to make: (i) narrowband searches using a phased-up, beamformed array, extending the commensal model pioneered for the VLA and MeerKAT into a regime where drift rates reach ~ 103 Hz s^-1; (ii) broadband aggregate leakage (BRaTs) from Kardashev Type I civilisations, for which 128-512 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth places a ~ 60 pc horizon within an integration time of one hour on source; (iii) Dysonian searches for the cold waste heat of computation - Slysh haloes - whose arcsecond and subarcsecond angular scales around M dwarfs are well matched to ALMA2040's array configuration; and (iv) geometric discontinuities imprinted by occulting megastructures, detectable as ringing in the visibility function with a phased ALMA operating in a mm/sub-mm VLBI array. We set out the corresponding requirements: bandwidth, beamforming, commensal access, spectral resolution and sub-second time resolution.

title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
authors: Ismail Cosandal, Sennur Ulukus, Nail Akar
abstract: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

title: FPG-Seg: Annotation-free Retinal Vessel Topology Segmentation
authors: James Willoughby, Irina Voiculescu
abstract: State-of-the art approaches to retinal vessel segmentation typically require extensive annotations, a highly time-consuming process, reliant on clinical expertise. We present FPG-Seg, an annotation-free pipeline for retinal vessel segmentation combining classical vesselness filtering, Bayesian deep learning and topology-aware graph reconstruction to segment retinal vessel topology without manual labels. Tested across four widely used benchmark datasets for retinal vessel segmentation, FPG-Seg attains a clDice of $0.74{-}0.78$, representing $86{-}98\%$ of the performance of an equivalent fully-supervised baseline, despite using no manual annotations for training or hyperparameter tuning. As part of this work, we also provide, to our knowledge, the first performance benchmark of an annotation-free vessel segmentation method on FIVES.

title: Deterministic Determination of Axial Constants, Sectional Regularities and Annihilator Numbers
authors: Amir Hashemi, Rozhin Sadr, Werner M. Seiler
abstract: Axial constants and sectional regularities are recently introduced invariants of homogeneous polynomial ideals that, like the already earlier introduced annihilator numbers, depend on generic choices of coordinates. We provide effective characterisations of the genericity underlying these invariants in terms of $β$-maximal position and strong stability. In particular, we show that $β$-maximal position suffices for determining generic annihilator numbers and sectional regularities, while its combination with strong stability yields corresponding results for axial constants. We also develop deterministic linear algebra procedures for detecting the required generic positions and for computing these invariants.

title: An infinite completely normal basis theorem
authors: Patrik Lundström
abstract: Let $L/K$ be an arbitrary Galois extension with group $G$, equipped with the Krull topology. Let $C(G,K)$ denote the $K$-vector space of continuous functions $G\to K$, with $K$ discrete and $G$ acting by left translation. We prove that there exists a $G$-equivariant $K$-linear isomorphism $\varphi:C(G,K)\to L$ such that, for every open subgroup $H$ of $G$, the map $\varphi^H:C(H,L^H)\to L$ induced by extension by zero and extension of scalars is an $H$-equivariant $L^H$-linear isomorphism. This gives a completely normal analogue of Lenstra's infinite normal basis theorem; the case of finite base fields was previously established in an equivalent form by Hachenberger.

title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
authors: Elena Wittemyer, Graco Gao
abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.

title: Generalization Guarantees of Randomized Block Coordinate Descent for Nonconvex Learning
authors: Ruixi Hu, Liang Wu
abstract: Randomized block coordinate descent (RBCD) is a popular optimization algorithm for many large-scale machine learning problems. The existing theoretical analysis of RBCD mainly focuses on its convergence behavior from an optimization perspective, while its generalization behavior remains less understood for nonconvex problems. In this paper, we establish high-probability generalization guarantees for RBCD with nonconvex objectives. In the general nonconvex setting, we derive bounds on the gradients of both empirical and population risks, requiring only standard smoothness assumptions. With polynomially decaying step sizes, we tune the iteration number to balance optimization and generalization, thereby quantifying how early stopping leads to the optimal convergence rate for the population gradients. In the gradient-dominated setting, we provide bounds in terms of functional suboptimality, which nearly match the optimistic rates in convex and low-noise settings. Finally, we develop dimension-independent bounds for loss functions of a specific structure, making the generalization guarantees applicable to high-dimensional problems.

title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity Enforcement for Thin-Structure Segmentation
authors: Junho Moon, Ikbeom Jang
abstract: Thin, elongated structures are particularly sensitive to connectivity errors, as even a few local segmentation mistakes can disrupt otherwise continuous paths. Existing skeleton-based objectives typically supervise fixed centerline locations and do not account for alternative local routes that may restore connectivity. We propose TRACE, a topology-aware, prediction-adaptive objective that uses a target skeleton to define required local connections. For each connection, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and jointly supervises its bottleneck with the corresponding skeleton point. The supervision thus adapts to the evolving prediction rather than remaining fixed to the centerline. We further introduce a topology-aware skeleton carrier that preserves both foreground and class-specific topology, enabling reliable definition of these connections. Extensive experiments across six 2D and 3D benchmarks show that TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong segmentation accuracy with low training overhead. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Gradient-Hessian Query Tradeoffs: Matching Lower Bounds in Logarithmic Dimension
authors: Wendao Wu, Haihan Zhang, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
abstract: We establish matching lower bounds for the tradeoff between gradient and Hessian queries in nonconvex optimization with Lipschitz Hessian. In normalized units, the initial objective gap is at most $T$, the Hessian Lipschitz constant is at most one, and the target gradient norm is one. For sufficiently large $T$, dimension $d \ge C\log(2+T)$, and a prescribed Hessian budget $h \ge 1$ with $h+1 \le aT$, every randomized algorithm requires $Ω(\min\{Td^{1/3}, T^{3/2}/\sqrt{h+1}\})$ ordinary queries. An ordinary query returns the value and gradient; a Hessian query returns the complete second jet and is charged only to its own budget. Both budgets are worst-case caps. Queries and outputs may be arbitrary real points, and no Hessian-norm bound is imposed. The hard input law consists of fixed, globally $C^3$, coercive functions. The construction combines sequential readouts of a continuous random matrix with localized completion blocks and reliability dimensions that vary across hierarchy levels. Premature disclosures are charged by their expected task cost, while every oracle reply remains the exact jet of the presampled objective. This yields a logarithmic dimension threshold and a depth-independent third-derivative bound. Together with a translation of the NALEN upper bound of Chen, Liu, Luo, and Zhang, the result determines the query tradeoff up to absolute constants throughout the stated range.

title: Learning Variable Metrics for Convergent Proximal Splitting Algorithms
authors: Yodai Suzuki, Shunsuke Ono
abstract: We propose learned variable metric (LVM), a framework that learns metrics of proximal splitting algorithms adapted to each problem instance, coordinate, and iteration with a convergence guarantee. Proximal splitting algorithms can solve a wide variety of convex optimization problems but often require many iterations to converge. Choosing a suitable metric is an effective remedy, and variable metric theory naturally extends convergence guarantees to metrics that vary over the iterations. Learning is a promising way to design such adaptive metrics beyond the reach of manual design, but a naive implementation leads to (i) an expensive evaluation of a network at every iteration and (ii) difficulty in satisfying the conditions that the theory imposes on the whole infinite sequence of metrics. To resolve these difficulties, we first train a neural network to generate a few representative metrics once per problem instance, and then obtain the metric of every iteration by combining them with basis functions of the normalized iteration index. We present LVM for the proximal gradient method with a quadratic term and the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, and prove their convergence under a mild spectral condition, which is ensured by a rescaling of the representative metrics. In experiments on deblurring and inpainting, LVM reduces the number of iterations to reach a target accuracy in most tested settings compared with several baselines, and the computation time at high accuracies.

title: OpenGCUA: Toward a Fully Open Stack for Generalist Computer Use
authors: Hanzhang Zhou, Long Li, Quyu Kong, Lei Wang, Panrong Tong, Long Chen, Tianyu Xia, Gongjie Zhang, Xu Zhang, Chen Liu, Jianan Zhang, Chenglin Cai, Zhengwen Zeng, Steven Hoi, Yue Wang
abstract: Computer use has reached a turning point: the focus is expanding from GUI-only interaction to systems that complete tasks on users' computers through visual and programmatic interfaces. We define a generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) as a system in which the model chooses how to observe, act, and organize its work across visual and programmatic interfaces. Yet frontier implementations, such as GPT-6 Astra's computer-use system, remain largely closed, limiting systematic study of their design. We introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for GCUAs with the community. This report presents the first release of OpenGCUA. Code execution is a key feature of our agent design: it lets intermediate results determine subsequent operations and enables models to apply their existing programming capabilities directly to computer interaction. We also propose harness-to-model decision transfer, moving selected observations and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On OSWorld-v2, our full configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, raising mean partial score by +19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. We release our implementation and prompts, evaluation trajectories from all eight models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The harness addresses real-device challenges not fully captured by benchmarks, while the SDK provides a common programming interface across computers, mobiles and browsers. Across four real macOS tasks under our real-device harness, selected Qwen3.8-Max runs use 19.4 times as many reported reasoning tokens as GPT-6 Astra, highlighting substantial differences between models in real-device execution efficiency.

title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation
authors: João Santos, Jayshankar Nath, Marco Pezzutto, Valentin Savin, Tristan Meunier, Yasser Omar
abstract: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.

title: The role of friction on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and numerical experiments
authors: Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo
abstract: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.

title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
authors: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.

title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures
authors: Guido Lagos, Simón Ávila
abstract: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once. As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets. We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain. This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies. We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely. Under the Lévy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass. Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.
